turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Bit of a wait, I'm afraid. The computer out front's been on the blink all morning. You're in with Dr Patel.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Um, sorry I'm late as well. The car park was heaving and I went in the wrong door.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in, have a seat. One second, this screen's frozen again. Right. What brings you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I nearly didn't come, if I'm honest. My neighbour said I was making a fuss over nothing, and I thought, well...
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? A warning just popped up and I lost you.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I found a lump. In the shower. Left breast. It doesn't hurt, it's just there.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): A lump in the left breast. When did you notice it? Any pain with it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Err. Ten days? Or it might've been a fortnight. I can't pin the day, I keep changing my mind.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Sorry, the screen's jumped. Say the timing once more?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): About ten days to two weeks, I really don't know the day. And no pain, none at all. I've been poking it, which I shouldn't, and I feel like a wet rag I'm that tired.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wet rag. Sorry, what do you mean? I was typing.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired. Wiped out. I can barely sleep. At work I can't hear myself think, the office is that loud, but that's just the open plan, it's not why I'm here.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Any discharge from the nipple?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing coming out. I checked.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the other breast?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that side feels normal. It's only the left. My mum had breast cancer, she was fifty-five.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mother, breast cancer at fifty-five. Any regular medicines? Slowly please, I've got the wrong tab open.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Sertralene, fifty milligrams, a couple of years for the anxiety. I take it at night, no, hang on, it's the morning, once in the morning.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sertraline, 50 milligrams, every morning. Do you actually take it every day?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. I've missed a few this month, three or four. I've been all over the place.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A little white tablet the other GP started. I can't remember the name, blood pressure or cholesterol, I've no idea. It's just small and white.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): No name then. How old are you? It's blank on here.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty-three. Is it cancer though, my mum's was, will they take the breast off? Should I ring my sister tonight, and what if I've overdone it just from all the checking?

[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you, lie back, then I'll answer what I can. Firm lump in the left breast, upper outer part, about 2 centimetres, and the skin looks normal, nothing pulling in. Right breast is clear. Both armpits are clear.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): 2 centimetres, is that big? If the armpits are clear, has it not spread? I walk most evenings, forty minutes or so, am I still allowed?
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can't tell you it hasn't spread, and the size doesn't settle what it is. It might be benign, a cyst, but I can't rule out a cancer.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So it might be cancer. What happens now?
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the walking going, that's fine. Stop poking the lump. I'm referring you on the urgent two-week breast pathway, and that is going ahead, not a maybe.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok, I'll keep walking and I'll stop poking it. Do I stop the sertralene, and the white tablet? Two weeks feels endless when you can't sleep.

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the sertraline. Bring me the white tablet's box so we can read the name. If the skin goes red, or you get a fever, or it starts to break down, come back sooner, don't wait.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll bring the box. Will they scan it there? What if it's nothing and I've wasted the slot?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): The clinic does the scans. I can't call it nothing from today, that's why you're going.
[SEG0034] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Stop at the desk and I'll send the urgent breast referral through now. You should get a date inside the fortnight.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Sorry, my head's been full of questions.

spec.situation: Woman in her forties who found a painless lump in the left breast in the shower; no nipple discharge; mother had breast cancer at fifty-five; examination described; urgent clinic referral.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Dose, morning, anxiety, current use supported; duration applies to anxiety/usage context, not explicitly the medication.
bad.text: sertraline (dose=50 mg, frequency=once daily in the morning, duration=approximately 2 years, indication=anxiety, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Sertraline adherence detail: patient takes it most days but has missed three or four doses this month.
Doctor advised to come back sooner and not wait for the 2-week appointment if the breast skin goes red, if she develops fever, or if the area starts to break down.
Clinical staff said the urgent breast referral would be sent immediately and the patient should receive an appointment date within the fortnight.
